title: Detection of Client Configurations
summary: This detection strategy covers the gathering of client configurations, the technique where an adversary learns how target users work before crafting a lure or an exploit: browser and operating system versions, installed extensions and plug ins, virtual private network clients, mail clients and the scripts a public web page runs in the visitor's browser. It matters because it converts a general attack into a precise one, and the collection is split between off network activity the victim cannot see and on network activity that looks similar to ordinary browsing if you only review single requests. The telemetry that makes it possible is secure web gateway logs with the user agent string, version fingerprinting endpoints served by the organisation or by a lure page, endpoint management inventory reports, and public site analytics that show one address visiting the same page with many different fingerprints. Detection fails because user agents vary across the estate and version checks are built into normal web browsing.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for someone learning how your users work. The attacker wants to know which browser, which programs and which versions people use. The rule watches for pages that collect browser details, called fingerprinting. It also watches for many different browser strings arriving from one address.
beginner.whyItMatters: An exploit works only on specific versions. Knowing your versions lets the attacker send a lure that matches. Users notice nothing, because the page looks like an ordinary web page. Catching the collection early helps you warn the right group of staff.
howItWorks: Browsers send a user agent string with every web request. That string names the browser, the version and the system.
A web gateway or proxy logs the string, the requested page, the address and the signed in user.
Fingerprinting pages are known by their address, because they collect screen size, installed fonts and plug in lists.
The rule selects requests to those pages and groups them by the requesting address or user.
It counts how many different user agent strings one site receives from one address in a short window.
A single external address visiting your pages with many fingerprints is treated as collection, not normal use.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital sign in sheet that records the name, the ward and the shift of every visitor. The sheet helps staff. However, a visitor who reads the whole sheet learns when each ward is quiet. This detection watches who reads the whole sheet.
takeaways: Version detail is worth more to an attacker than a name, because it selects the tool.
Fingerprinting usually hides behind an ordinary looking web page.
One external address showing many browser versions is a strong sign of collection.

objectives: Explain how client configuration detail improves a targeted attack.
Identify the proxy, endpoint and web server fields that record fingerprinting.
Write a rule that counts distinct user agent strings per external address.
Describe how to inventory browser and plug in versions across the estate.
Explain why ordinary browsing makes this detection noisy without a baseline.
dataSources: Secure web gateway and proxy logs recording the user agent string, requested host, full uniform resource locator and user
Web server and content delivery logs for corporate sites showing one address requesting fingerprinting scripts repeatedly
Endpoint management inventory reports listing operating system build, browser version and installed browser extensions
Endpoint detection and response telemetry showing browser plug in installation and version change events
Domain name system resolver logs for known browser fingerprinting and device detection services
logic: The pattern is one external address, or one internal account, producing an unusually wide spread of user agent strings and client capability data against the same page or endpoint in a short window, or a burst of requests to known fingerprinting and device detection services that the organisation does not use for its own applications. The fields that must be correlated are the requesting address, the distinct user agent strings and their count, the requested fingerprinting endpoints, the authenticated user where the traffic is internal, and the endpoint inventory of browser and plug in versions. The benign case is web analytics, banks and content delivery networks that fingerprint every visitor as part of fraud protection; the malicious case is a single hosting address visiting a lure page with many constructed user agents to test which browser version the target group runs, or an internal account opening a fingerprinting page that no business process uses.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Browser Fingerprinting Endpoint Contacted From Public Site
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: web_proxy
# detection:
#   selection:
#     url|contains:
#       - 'fingerprint.js'
#       - 'device-detect'
#       - 'browser-check'
#   filter_apps:
#     user|endswith:
#       - 'fraud-tools'
#       - 'analytics'
#   condition: selection and not filter_apps | count(distinct user_agent) by src_ip > 8 within 30m
# level: low
falsePositives: Fraud prevention and bot management scripts that collect browser detail on every visitor to a public site
Application testing teams that replay requests with many user agent strings as part of browser support work
Content delivery networks that record client capability data to choose a cached asset version
An internal help desk that asks users to open a browser check page to confirm their version before an upgrade
tuningNotes: Allow list the fingerprinting services used by your own web applications and by your payment or fraud providers, then scope the rule to corporate web traffic and to your public site logs separately. Baseline user agent diversity per address for thirty days and alert on addresses whose spread is far above the peer group rather than on a fixed number. Update the list of fingerprinting endpoints quarterly, because new services appear often. This filter loses coverage of an attacker who uses an unknown or self hosted fingerprinting page, so pair the rule with a monthly report of the top user agent strings per external address and review any address that shows more than twenty.
